sections.title: Objective type questions (2 parts of 1 mark, or 4 parts of ½ mark).

questions.q: Complete the sentences: (I) Indian soldiers in the East India Company's army were not given promotion above that of ____. (II) A sepoy called ____ was the first soldier who openly disobeyed British orders.
questions.answer: (I) subedar (II) Mangal Pandey

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: At Kanpur ____ was declared the Peshwa, and his troops were commanded by ____ and Azimullah.
questions.answer: Nana Saheb; Tantya Tope

questions.q: Answer in one word each: (a) Which tribal leader died in prison in 1900? (b) Which Act of 1908 gave tribals some land ownership rights and banned bonded labour?
questions.answer: (a) Birsa Munda (b) The Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act

questions.q: True or False: (a) The Revolt of 1857 spread equally to all parts of India, including Punjab and the Madras Presidency. (b) The Indigo Rebellion forced the government to declare compulsory indigo cultivation illegal in 1860.
questions.answer: (a) False — it was confined mainly to North and Central India. (b) True

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: The Jaintia leader ____ was publicly hanged and the Garo leader ____ was defeated by the British.
questions.answer: U Kiang Nongbah; Pa Togan Sangma

questions.q: Match: (a) Rani Lakshmi Bai (b) Khan Bahadur Khan (c) Bahadur Shah Zafar (d) Wahabi Movement — (i) Delhi (ii) Syed Ahmed Barelvi (iii) Jhansi (iv) Bareilly
questions.answer: (a) – (iii) Jhansi; (b) – (iv) Bareilly; (c) – (i) Delhi; (d) – (ii) Syed Ahmed Barelvi

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Explain any two reasons for the growing discontent among farmers growing indigo during British rule.
questions.answer: (1) They were paid very low prices for indigo by the planters. (2) Indigo had to be sown at the same time as food crops and it reduced the fertility of the soil, so food production fell.

or.q: Name the leader of the Wahabi movement and explain the significance of the movement.
or.answer: It was led by Syed Ahmed Barelvi of Rae Bareli. Though religious in origin, it became a class struggle in which peasants, irrespective of religion, united against their landlords, adding to anti-British feeling.

questions.q: Describe the Jaintia and Garo Rebellion in brief.
questions.answer: After the First Anglo-Burmese War the British planned a strategic road from the Brahmaputra valley to Sylhet. The Jaintias and Garos of present Meghalaya opposed it from 1827; the British burnt their villages and the anger grew with new house and income taxes in the 1860s. Jaintia leader U Kiang Nongbah was hanged and Garo leader Pa Togan Sangma defeated.

questions.q: Explain one social and one religious cause of the Revolt of 1857.
questions.answer: Social: reforms such as the ban on sati, widow remarriage and women's education were seen as interference in Indian customs, and Indians were treated with contempt. Religious: missionary schools and Act XXI of 1850 (which let converts inherit property) made people fear forced conversion; sepoys feared losing caste by crossing the sea.

questions.q: List two grievances of the Indian sepoys against the British.
questions.answer: (1) They were paid less than English soldiers, could not rise above subedar and were often denied bhatta for overseas service. (2) Their religious feelings were hurt — they were ordered to remove caste marks, serve overseas, and finally to use greased cartridges.

questions.q: Why is the Revolt of 1857 called the first national struggle for independence?
questions.answer: (1) Though begun by the sepoys, it was joined by peasants, artisans and others, and people of many regions fought together against the British. (2) It was marked by Hindu–Muslim unity — the rebels even proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar as Emperor of India. It sowed the seeds of nationalism and gave India heroes.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain the causes of the early resistance movements against British rule in India before the Revolt of 1857.
questions.answer: (1) British policies took away the rights, status and land of displaced rulers, zamindars and poligars. (2) Heavy land revenue, eviction and exploitation by moneylenders and forced commercial crops ruined peasants. (3) Tribals lost their land and forests to traders and moneylenders. (4) Interference in religious practices angered people. They aimed to restore old structures and resist outside interference.

or.q: Explain the causes of the revolt of the Poligars of Madras.
or.answer: The Poligars were local chiefs in the Madras Presidency who held military and land rights. When the British tried to take away these rights, disband their armed retainers and collect revenue directly, they lost their power and income, so they rebelled; the British crushed them.

questions.q: Describe the Faqir and Sanyasi Rebellions of 1770–1820s.
questions.answer: After British control of Bengal, land revenue rose and the Bengal famine of 1770 caused misery. Peasants whose land was confiscated, displaced zamindars and disbanded soldiers joined the Sanyasis and Faqirs (wandering Muslim mendicants). Leaders like Majnum Shah, Bhawani Pathak and Devi Choudhurani attacked English factories and seized goods and arms; restrictions on pilgrims were the immediate cause. The British crushed them by the early 19th century.

questions.q: Explain four reasons why the peasants revolted against British rule.
questions.answer: (1) High land revenue under the Permanent, Ryotwari and Mahalwari settlements. (2) Loss of land to moneylenders (mahajans) charging high interest, making peasants bonded labourers. (3) Forced cultivation of commercial crops like indigo at low prices, reducing food and causing famines. (4) Harassment by officials, zamindars and middlemen and no access to justice.

questions.q: Why did the Revolt of 1857 fail? Explain.
questions.answer: (1) No unity of purpose: leaders fought for their own territories — the Mughal throne, the Peshwaship, Jhansi. (2) It was confined to North and Central India; Punjab, Rajputana, Madras and Bombay stayed away and many rulers and the educated classes helped the British. (3) Weak leadership, poor planning and lack of coordination. (4) Shortage of modern weapons and money, while the British had the telegraph and control of the sea.

questions.q: Explain the impact of the Revolt of 1857 on India.
questions.answer: (1) East India Company rule ended and the Crown took direct control (1858). (2) The army was reorganised with more Europeans and fewer Indians; Indian artillery was disbanded. (3) The British followed 'Divide and Rule' between Hindus and Muslims. (4) Indian rulers were assured of their states and right of adoption. (5) It sowed the seeds of nationalism and gave India national heroes.

questions.q: Describe the Munda Rebellion and its significance.
questions.answer: The Mundas, the original clearers of the forest, enjoyed special land rights, which were destroyed by merchants, moneylenders and British contractors who made them indentured labourers. Birsa Munda, who had some missionary education, led them (1899–1900), attacked police stations and churches, and urged them to protect their sacred groves. He died in prison in 1900, but the Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act (1908) gave tribals land rights and banned bonded labour.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Describe the political, economic, social and military causes of the Revolt of 1857.
questions.answer: Political: (1) Doctrine of Lapse and Subsidiary Alliance annexed states like Satara, Nagpur and Jhansi; Nana Saheb was denied his pension and Awadh was annexed, leaving soldiers and officials jobless. Economic: (2) Handicrafts were ruined and wealth drained; (3) heavy land revenue made peasants lose land to moneylenders, and famines followed. Social-religious: (4) reforms and missionary activity and Act XXI of 1850 made people fear conversion. Military: (5) sepoys were paid less, denied promotion and bhatta, and forced to serve overseas. Immediate: (6) greased cartridges believed to contain cow and pig fat hurt both Hindus and Muslims.

questions.q: Explain the nature and significance of the Revolt of 1857.
questions.answer: (1) It began as a revolt of sepoys but was joined by peasants, artisans and rulers, so it became a popular revolt. (2) Hindus and Muslims, landlords and peasants fought together against a common enemy. (3) Rebels of different regions helped each other; it is called the First War of Independence. (4) It ended the East India Company's rule and the Crown took over in 1858. (5) The British changed their army and policies, adopting Divide and Rule. (6) Though it failed, it sowed the seeds of nationalism and inspired later struggles.
